newsitem.title: SPAIN: Baltics cheered by support of NATO's new members.
newsitem.headline: Baltics cheered by support of NATO's new members.

text.p: The three central European countries invited into NATO stretched out a helping hand to the Baltic states on Wednesday in support of their bid to join the alliance despite fierce Russian opposition.

Leaders from Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic clasped hands with the presidents of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia in a symbolic gesture after promising to fight for the Baltic cause within the North Atlantic Alliance.
The Kremlin has said it would consider it a threat to its security if the Baltic states, former Soviet republics with substantial Russian minorities, joined NATO.
But the three states were undeterred, and Latvian President Guntis Ulmanis said he hoped they would be in NATO within seven years.
"I think we will join in the near future, within the next five to seven years," he told reporters on the margins of a NATO summit in Madrid.
NATO invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to join the Western alliance on Tuesday but the Baltic states were excluded from the first wave of enlargement.
However, the three former Soviet bloc states promised to support the Baltics in their aspirations for future membership.
"There are no dividing lines, we are all supporting each other," Latvian ambassador to NATO, Juri Lunk, told reporters.
A senior U.S. diplomat also supported the Baltics' case, saying Washington did not consider NATO enlargement complete or successful until the three ex-Soviet republics were included.

"We will work with each of the three Baltic states to help them achieve their goal of becoming members of NATO," U.S. ambassador to Sweden Thomas Siebert said in a Swedish daily. "We will also support their desire to become EU members."
Lithuanian parliament chairman Vytautas Landsbergis took exception to the fact that in the final summit declaration the three were not mentioned by name but only as the Baltic region.
However, he broadly welcomed the summit's conclusion. "The declaration is a real step to the increased security of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia," he said in a statement.
Estonian President Lennart Meri said he hoped the Baltics would be considered in the next wave of NATO expansion having made great strides in preparing themselves militarily and economically.

"I ... believe that when the time comes for taking decisions on whom to invite for the next round, Estonia and its two Baltic neighbours will be among the most serious candidates," he said in remarks prepared for delivery in Madrid.
"I believe that it is fair to say that the Cold War will only finally be over when the Baltic countries have assumed their place behind the NATO Council Table," he said.
Estonia had been cheered by the NATO expansion text and the implications for the Baltic states.
"We were very encouraged by the strong open door language in the text...we feel safe enough," he added.
Meri would not rule out joining the European Union ahead of NATO, but said the decision was not in Estonia's hands.
Talks over European Union enlargement are expected to centre on five eastern countries including Estonia, according to draft European Commission documents.
But Meri declined to comment on what he thought his country's chances were. "It's not my decision, but we're happy that a number of reports have suggested that we will be in the first wave," he said.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Tuesday denounced NATO's expansion into former Communist eastern Europe as the worst mistake on the continent since World War Two.
But the three small nations, independent from Moscow's rule since 1991, are eager to join NATO as they seek permanent protection in case Russia leaves the path of democracy and turns hostile again.
